I have farmed this land 30 years, so I will start from what I did before and only move a little. On my 6.5 mu, wheat and maize are one after the other on the same land, so I count the full 6.5 mu for wheat season and the full 6.5 mu again for maize season. I do not like taking chances with fertilizer. If I put a little extra, I lose some money. If I put too little and the yield drops, that hurts much more. Around here, I will follow what works on other people’s fields and what has given me steady harvests. With well water, I can keep the crop from suffering when it turns dry, so I will not save too much on irrigation.

For wheat, I will use improved seed, because the old kinds do not hold yield well now. I will rotary till after maize, put most of the phosphate and potash in as base fertilizer, and split the nitrogen: one part at sowing, one part at jointing. I will give 16 kg nitrogen, 7 kg phosphorus, and 5 kg potassium per mu. I will irrigate 3 times if the year is normal: once after sowing if the soil is dry, once at jointing, once at grain filling if needed. I will spray 2 times, one for weeds and one for disease or aphids if they come. If the weather is good, I will look for about 520 kg per mu.

For maize, I will also use hybrid seed because that is what gives grain on our side. After wheat harvest, I will move fast, rotary the land, sow, and put fertilizer down. I will give 15 kg nitrogen, 6 kg phosphorus, and 5 kg potassium per mu. Most of the phosphate and potash will go in first, and I will topdress nitrogen around the big bell-mouth stage. I will irrigate 2 times in a normal year, one after sowing if there is no rain and one around tasseling or grain filling. I will spray 2 times, one for weeds early and one for insects later. On good irrigated land, I will count on about 600 kg per mu.
